newsitem.title: UK: WEEK AHEAD - Investors to hang on Greenspan's words.
newsitem.headline: WEEK AHEAD - Investors to hang on Greenspan's words.

text.p: Global markets will hang on the every word of U.S. Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan in the week ahead, analysts said on Friday.

Greenspan will give his semi-annual Humphrey-Hawkins testimony to Congress on Tuesday and Wednesday. His comments will be the highlight of a busy week also featuring key data in the U.S., France, Japan and Canada.
"The Greenspan delivery in the Humphrey-Hawkins testimony is going to dominate markets around the world," said Stephen Lewis, director of research at London Bond Broking.

"He's going to say clearly the risks of inflation moving higher are greater than the risks of the economy slipping into recession," Lewis said. "I certainly wouldn't rule out an interest rate rise as early as March 25," Lewis said.

Last year, Greenspan made a remark questioning how authorities could determine when markets were showing "irrational exuberance," a comment which markets initially took as a warning and which sent bond and stock prices tumbling.

"The bond market is already a little bit concerned that he's going to warn again that the U.S. economy is growing above trend and inflation pressures are growing," said Kieth Edmunds, chief analyst at IBJ International.
"As a result of that, we could well see a tightening of monetary policy," he said.
However, some said the testimony could be a let-down.
"There has been so much talk about the Fed's position, and it hasn't changed really," said Adrian Schmidt, international economist at Chase here.
"To be honest, I doubt he's going to make anything clearer," Schmidt said. "It could be a bit of a non-event."
Analysts also said markets would be watching French growth, unemployment, trade and consumer spending data for hints of any uptrend in France's sluggish economic performance this year.
"French GDP will be close to unchanged, and unemployment will be steady on 12.7," Schmidt said.
A decline in the jobless number would be positive for the bonds despite showing economic strength, he said.
It would also add confidence in France's progress towards meeting European economic and monetary union (EMU) convergence criteria, Schmidt said.
Analysts said markets would also be watchful of February German inflation figures, due mid-week.
Edmunds predicted year-on-year inflation at 1.6 percent, down from 1.8 percent the prior month. That would relieve some of the pressure on the Bund market, he said.

Schmidt also said German Chancellor Helmut Kohl's meeting on Monday with opposition Social Democrat party boss Oskar Lafontaine to discuss tax reform could test Kohl's status and have repercussions on EMU confidence.
In Britain, a by-election for a parliamentary seat on Thursday that has the opposition Labour Party tipped to win, could jolt UK markets, Schmidt said.

It will be the last political contest before the general election. If the ruling Conservatives pull a surprise win, it could increase speculation of a hung parliament, which would be negative for sterling and British bonds, he said.
Japan will release January industrial production data on Thursday, followed by unemployment and consumer price numbers on Friday.
Canada will post fourth-quarter gross domestic product figures on Friday. --International Bonds Unit +44 171 542 6320
